options: A preventive measure that brings large benefit to the community offers little to each participating individual.
Interventions targeting high-risk individuals always prevent more cases than population-wide measures.
Preventing disease is, paradoxically, more expensive than treating it.
Individuals at the highest risk gain the least from preventive interventions.
rationale: Rose's paradox is that a measure delivering large benefit to a whole population often offers little perceptible benefit to each individual taking part, which weakens individual motivation. It is a central argument for population-level rather than purely high-risk strategies.

stem: A key advantage of Rose's population strategy over the high-risk strategy is that it:
options: Requires screening to identify everyone above a defined risk threshold.
Shifts the whole distribution of risk, addressing the many cases that arise from the large number of people at moderate risk.
Concentrates resources on the small number of individuals at greatest risk.
Avoids the need for any structural or environmental change.
rationale: The population strategy aims to move the entire risk distribution downwards. Because most cases often arise from the many people at small-to-moderate risk rather than the few at high risk, it can prevent more cases overall. The high-risk strategy, by contrast, screens for and targets individuals above a threshold.

stem: A national breast cancer screening programme is an example of which type of prevention?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention
rationale: Screening detects disease at an early, often presymptomatic stage so it can be treated sooner: this is secondary prevention. Primary prevention stops disease arising at all (e.g. immunisation); tertiary prevention reduces the impact or complications of established disease (e.g. cardiac rehabilitation).

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes incidence from prevalence?
options: Incidence counts existing cases; prevalence counts new cases.
Incidence measures new cases arising over a period; prevalence measures all existing cases at a given time.
Incidence and prevalence are interchangeable measures of disease frequency.
Prevalence applies only to infectious disease; incidence only to chronic disease.
rationale: Incidence is the rate of new cases in a population over a defined period. Prevalence is the proportion with the condition at a point (or over a period) in time, so it reflects both incidence and how long the condition lasts.

stem: In the Dahlgren and Whitehead “rainbow” model, which of these layers sits closest to the individual?
options: General socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions
Living and working conditions
Social and community networks
Individual lifestyle factors
rationale: Moving outward from fixed factors at the centre (age, sex, hereditary factors), the model runs: individual lifestyle factors, then social and community networks, then living and working conditions, with general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions as the outer layer. Outer layers shape the inner ones.

stem: Marmot's phrase “the causes of the causes” refers to:
options: The biological mechanisms linking risk factors to disease.
The underlying social and economic conditions that shape exposure to proximal risk factors.
Genetic predispositions that cause chronic disease.
The direct behavioural choices individuals make day to day.
rationale: Marmot points upstream from proximal risk factors such as smoking or diet to the social determinants: the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, which shape those risk factors in the first place.

stem: Legislating to remove industrial trans fats from the food supply is a clean example of a population-level intervention because it:
options: Targets only individuals already diagnosed with cardiovascular disease.
Lowers cardiovascular risk across the whole population without requiring individuals to change their behaviour.
Relies on individuals correctly interpreting food labels.
Has no measurable effect on population health outcomes.
rationale: Removing industrial trans fats shifts the population's risk downwards through a structural change to the food environment, with no demand on individual behaviour or motivation. This sidesteps the prevention paradox's main weakness and makes the healthier option the default.

options: Providing every group with identical resources regardless of need.
The absence of avoidable, unfair and remediable differences in health between population groups.
Ensuring that all health outcomes are statistically identical.
A synonym for health equality.
rationale: Equity concerns the fairness of differences: those that are avoidable, unfair and remediable, often addressed by allocating resources according to need. Equality (identical resources or outcomes) is a different idea and can entrench disadvantage.
